intent: Establish that the software does what it claims by automated evidence distributed across unit, integration and end-to-end layers in a shape that stays fast, deterministic and maintainable.
problem: Correctness is asserted informally — a reviewer says it looks right, a demo passes once — so defects are found in production by users. The alternative, testing everything end to end, is slow, flaky and so expensive that teams delete the tests instead of maintaining them, leaving less coverage than they started with.
context: The strategy question is not 'how many tests' but 'at which layer, in what proportion'. Mike Cohn's pyramid — many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, few end-to-end tests — survives because low-level tests are fast, precise and cheap, while high-level tests are slow, brittle and ambiguous when they fail. Modern practice (the testing trophy, the honeycomb) shifts the centre of gravity toward integration tests where the high-value composition bugs actually live, and the proportion is a starting point, not a law.
benefits: Defects are caught near the code that caused them, while the failure is still explainable.
Fast feedback on every commit, which is the precondition for continuous integration.
Refactoring is safe: a green suite is what makes behaviour-preserving change possible.
Test structure documents the intended behaviour in executable form.
Flakiness stays contained in the small number of high-level tests that need it.
tradeoffs: No amount of testing proves the absence of defects; coverage measures what was executed, not what was verified.
Over-mocking at the unit level produces tests that pass while the composition is broken — the classic unit-test mirage.
End-to-end tests remain necessary but are the most expensive and least reliable layer to own.
A pyramid-shaped suite that has collapsed into an ice-cream cone is worse than no strategy, because it looks like a strategy.
Layer boundaries chosen to make testing easy can distort the production design (testability-driven architecture debt).
quality_attributes_note: testability 10 by definition. security 8 because tests are the main evidence for input validation and authorisation paths; scalability 6 because a large suite constrains CI throughput.

participants.responsibility: Verifies one unit in isolation, fast and deterministic; the wide base of the suite.
participants.notes: Use real collaborators over mocks unless the collaborator is a boundary or nondeterministic.

participants.responsibility: Verifies that units compose correctly across real seams — database, message broker, HTTP.
participants.notes: This layer catches the bugs unit tests structurally cannot.

participants.responsibility: Verifies a critical user journey through the deployed system; few, slow, and maintained with care.
participants.notes: Reserve for the few flows whose failure would be a business incident.

participants.responsibility: The assertion that decides pass/fail; the part that is usually faked in a bad suite.
participants.notes: A test that restates the implementation proves nothing.

use_cases: Building a suite with many unit tests, a handful of integration tests against a real database, and a few end-to-end journeys.
Adding contract tests so two services can deploy independently without one blocking the other.
Adding property-based tests for parsers, codecs and anything with an inverse.
Replacing a slow end-to-end suite with integration tests that exercise components as a user would.
Adding characterisation tests before a risky refactor of untested legacy code.
avoid_when: Correctness is formally verified or proved (dependent types, model checking) — the proof is stronger and does not rot.
The property is not testable by an oracle: concurrency bugs and timing bugs need stress testing or determinism controls instead.
A prototype exists to answer one question; testing it delays the answer at no value.
Pure performance work, where a benchmark harness is the right instrument, not assertions.
pitfalls: Ice-cream-cone distribution: many UI/end-to-end tests, almost no unit tests.
Mocking the thing under test's own collaborators so thoroughly that the test asserts only that mocks were called.
Asserting on implementation details, which makes the test block every legitimate refactoring.
Sharing mutable fixtures across tests so the suite only passes in one order.
Chasing a coverage percentage — a suite can hit 100% coverage and assert nothing.
Flaky tests left in the suite with a retry, which trains the team to ignore failures.

related_patterns_notes.arrange-act-assert: The structural shape of every test case; the fastest way to make a test readable.
related_patterns_notes.characterization-test: Pins current behaviour before a refactor of code that has none, turning a rewrite into a safe step.
related_patterns_notes.consumer-driven-contract-test: Makes an integration seam verifiable on both sides so the boundary can be tested independently of deployment order.
related_patterns_notes.property-based-serializer: Where a property oracle is the right substitute for example-based assertions (round-trip, invariance).

anti_patterns: Assertion-free tests that only exercise code for coverage.
Sleeps instead of explicit synchronisation in concurrency tests.
Shared fixture state producing order-dependent results.
Mocking the framework or the language runtime.
Tying a unit test to a live third-party API so the suite fails when someone else deploys.
design_principles: Write tests at different granularities, and write fewer the higher the level (Fowler, The Practical Test Pyramid).
Stick to the pyramid shape: lots of small fast unit tests, some coarse-grained tests, very few high-level tests.
A good first guess is roughly 70/20/10 unit / integration / end-to-end, with the shape preserved even when the ratio varies.
Do not become so attached to the names of the layers; the pyramid is a rule of thumb about granularity and proportion.
Unit tests cannot give confidence that the application works with all the external parts it talks to — only integration tests can.
best_practices: Prefer integration tests over heavily-mocked unit tests for anything with real composition logic (Testing Library's guiding principle).
Make the suite fast enough that developers run it before every commit; otherwise it will not be run.
Quarantine and fix flaky tests rather than retrying them.
Assert on observable outcomes, not on internal call sequences.
Use contract tests to keep independently deployable services verifiable.
Treat the suite as the safety net that makes refactoring possible — it is infrastructure, not paperwork.
sources: Martin Fowler, The Practical Test Pyramid — https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html
